podcast.title: Grammy Performance of "Glitter in the Air" (2010)
podcast.body: On January 31, 2010, Pink delivered an acclaimed live performance of "Glitter in the Air" at the Grammy Awards. Starting on the stage, she was then lifted into the Staples Center rafters by silks, performing with a trio of fellow gymnasts, singing live throughout. By the song's climax, her body was doused in water, and she performed upside down, making this a regularly cited "greatest Grammy performance." "Pink performed Glitter in the Air live on the broadcast, starting from the Grammy stage. Then she lifted into the staple center rafters by silks held by a trio of fellow gymnasts."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Pregnancy Announcement (2010)
podcast.body: Pink announced her first pregnancy later in 2010, around the same time she was issuing her "Greatest Hits, So Far" compilation album. "Pink became pregnant with their first child later that year."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Continued Acrobatics (2023)
podcast.body: Pink, at 43 years old in 2023, confirmed that her live acrobatics would continue on her tour for the "Trust Fall" album, asking, "once you get to fly, why would you not?" "In her promotion for her new album, the 43-year-old Pink has already affirmed not only that she is going back on tour this year, but that her live acrobatics will continue."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: No Longer Misunderstood (2023)
podcast.body: After more than 20 years in the music industry, Pink is confident she is "not worried about" feeling misunderstood anymore. "It's been more than 20 years since Pink said she felt misunderstood. I'm pretty sure she's not worried about that anymore."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Ongoing Marriage (2023)
podcast.body: More than a decade after their reconciliation in 2010, Pink and Carey Hart remain married and have two children. "They are still married with two children more than a decade later."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "Blow Me" Title Tamed
podcast.body: After the controversy surrounding "F***ing Perfect," the title "Blow Me (One Last Kiss)" seemed "relatively tame to radio programmers," which allowed it to top radio playlists. "I guess after fucking perfect, Blow Me seemed relatively tame to radio programmers."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "Greatest Hits So Far" Chart Feat
podcast.body: Pink achieved a "virtually unprecedented chart feat" by having two new songs from a greatest hits album – "Raise Your Glass" (number one) and "F***ing Perfect" (number two) – become major hits, a rare occurrence for such compilations. "It was already remarkable that Pink had landed a new number one and a new number two from a greatest hits album, a virtually unprecedented chart feat."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "Pornopoparazzi Girls" Satire
podcast.body: Pink used the term "Pornopoparazzi Girls" to describe the mid-aughts reality show culture and Paris Hilton tabloid culture that she satirized in her song "Stupid Girls." "a rip on what pink called Pornopoparazzi Girls at the peak of Paris Hilton tabloid culture."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "Stupid Girls" Video Controversy
podcast.body: The music video for "Stupid Girls" generated controversy when a USA Today reporter intentionally sought comments from the celebrity women (Paris Hilton, Mary-Kate Olsen, Lindsay Lohan, Jessica Simpson) Pink was satirizing in the clip. "One USA Today reporter, Gind Up Controversy, by seeking comment from the starlet's pink was satirizing."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Consistent Sound Over 20+ Years
podcast.body: Pink's extensive list of hits is noted for its remarkable consistency in sound, despite evolving over two decades. Her songs are described as "vulnerable and defiant, self-deprecating and self-aggrandizing, rocking and soulful," embodying her unbranded style. "But the remarkable thing about Pink's long list of hits is how consistent they sound, how unbranded they are for her."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Early Career in Philadelphia Nightclubs
podcast.body: As a teenager, Pink was already performing in Philadelphia nightclubs. She secured a regular Friday singing slot after impressing the crowd at an open mic night with a Mary J. Blige song. She also served as a dancer and then a vocalist for local R&B acts like Schools of Thought and Basic Instinct, although she never recorded with them. "By her early teenage years, Alicia Moore, a troubled teen who, after her parents divorced, often ran away from home, was already performing at Philly Nightclubs."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Early Life and Nickname
podcast.body: Born Alicia Beth Moore in 1979 in Doylestown, Pennsylvania, to a Catholic father and Jewish mother. She developed a potent voice at an early age and focused on singing, not gymnastics (which would later become useful in her career). After her parents' divorce, she became a troubled teen who often ran away from home. One plausible origin story for her nickname "Pink" is that she was "the only white girl in her friend group." "Alicia Beth Moore, born in 1979 to a Catholic father and Jewish mother in the Philadelphia suburb of Doyle's Town, Pennsylvania, developed a potent voice at an early age."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Elaborate Gymnastic Performances
podcast.body: Beginning with her "I'm Not Dead" tour, Pink introduced elaborate gymnastic routines, including aerial silks, into her on-stage performances, which became a hallmark of her live shows, with audiences "gasping as pink spun from the arena's rafters." "adding elaborate gymnastic routines to her on-stage performances starting on the I'm Not Dead tour."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Genre Transformation
podcast.body: Pink successfully switched from R&B to pop, and then to a form of 21st-century rock music, effectively transforming herself into a self-styled rock star. "More recently, I explained how pink switched from R&B to pop, and then a kind of 21st century rock music becoming a self-styled rock star."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Individualism and Fighting the Record Label
podcast.body: Pink established her individualism by fighting her record label, LaFace Records, for creative control over her second album, "Missundaztood." She challenged the direction the label had set for her debut, which she felt misrepresented her true artistic identity. Despite label president L.A. Reid's belief that her new rock-oriented approach would be "commercial suicide," Pink persisted and ultimately was granted "the freedom to fail," an opportunity she appreciated. "This individualism was established two decades ago when Alicia Moore took on her record label, fought them to a draw and was told they would give her the freedom to fail."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Influence on Avril Lavigne and Pop-Rock Shift
podcast.body: Pink was "ahead of a shift in pop music" towards a more rock-oriented direction, anticipating the decline of Britney Spears and Backstreet Boys-style teen pop. Her album "Missundaztood" opened up the market for artists like Avril Lavigne, who was signed by L.A. Reid around the same time Pink was working on her second album. Lavigne's album "Let Go" then blew up months after "Missundaztood" dropped. "In essence, Pink had opened up the market for Avril."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Lack of Rock Chart Presence
podcast.body: Despite her strong rock influence, multiple rock-leaning albums, and even winning a Grammy for Best Female Rock Vocal Performance for "Trouble," Pink, like Madonna, has never made Billboard's rock tracks charts. This is "fairly remarkable" as few female pop stars of her generation have integrated rock into popular music more than Pink, and the average fan often describes her as a rocker. "Pink, however, like Madonna, has not. This is fairly remarkable because few female pop stars of her generation have done more to integrate rock back into post-millennial, post-hip hop popular music than Pink."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Madonna as an Inspiration and Encounter
podcast.body: Pink cited Madonna as a significant inspiration for her willingness to take risks and evolve her sound. In a later interview, Pink expressed admiration for Madonna's career longevity and ability to change styles successfully. Recently, Pink discussed meeting Madonna with Howard Stern, clarifying that while she loves Madonna, the narrative that she was "fan-girling" was twisted, as Madonna had actually invited Pink into her dressing room. "That's why Madonna has always been an inspiration for me."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Marketed as Racially Ambiguous
podcast.body: For her debut album, "Can't Take Me Home," LaFace Records intentionally presented Pink in a way that made her ethnicity hard to discern, marketing her as a "hip hop diva in training" and "racially ambiguous." This strategy "worked on the charts," and cultural critics like Ashley Reese of Jezebel, in an article titled "Soulful Vanilla Child, When Pink Was Black," commented on how Pink's "black adjacent presentation worked on the charts." "On the cover, in an overlit photo, the 20-year-old pink wore reflective sunglasses and very close cropped hair, a look that made her ethnicity hard to discern."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Marriage Saved by "Funhouse" Album
podcast.body: Pink's "unfiltered marriage on the rocks album" ("Funhouse") is suggested to have contributed to saving her marriage with Carey Hart, as they confirmed their reconciliation in February 2010. "pinks unfiltered marriage on the rocks album may have saved her marriage."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Mid-2000s Regrouping
podcast.body: Following the poor commercial response to her album "Try This," Pink spent 2004 and 2005 "wood shedding material" and regrouping for her subsequent album. "Disguised by the poor response to try this, pink regrouped in 2004 and 2005, wood shedding material for her next album."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Multiple Imperial Phases
podcast.body: Pink experienced an early flurry of top 10s between 2000 and 2002, which could be argued as imperial. However, her more impressive imperial run occurred from 2010 to 2013, during which she scored five or more top 10s, many of which went top 5, and two of which hit number 1, establishing "a whole new level of imperiality" and "her own lane on the radio." "But arguably, her more impressive run came later from 2010 to 2013, when an older, savvier Pink scored 5 more top 10s, most of which went top 5 and 2 of which even hit number 1."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Material Girl in an Imperial World Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Music as Therapy
podcast.body: Pink views music as a form of therapy, which was evident when she channeled her personal pain from her trial separation from husband Carey Hart into the defiant song "So What." "A great believer in music as therapy, pink sank her hurt feelings into the defiant song, on which she literally calls herself a rock star."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Olympic Gymnast Ambition
podcast.body: Before becoming a singer, Pink had aspirations of being an Olympic gymnast. "I wanted to be an Olympic gymnast before I was a singer."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Original Millennial Pop Rock Hybridizer
podcast.body: In the mid-aughts, Pink was seen as the original millennial pop rock hybridizer, a designation that seemed vindicated by new hybrids of rock and pop dominating the radio charts. "the radio in the mid-Auts seemed to vindicate pink, the original millennial pop rock hybridizer."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Persona Defined by "You and Your Hand"
podcast.body: The song "You and Your Hand" is cited as the perfect encapsulation of what would become Pink's enduring persona: "a foul mouthed take-no-shit attitude paired with life-affirming music." "It was the perfect encapsulation of what would become the pink persona, a foul mouthed take-no-shit attitude paired with life-affirming music."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Reluctant Collaboration with Max Martin & Dr. Luke
podcast.body: Pink initially turned down the song "Since U Been Gone" from Max Martin and Dr. Luke, and later "reluctantly agreed" to work with them on songs for "I'm Not Dead" after her label's suggestion. "But when her label suggested they work together on songs for I'm Not Dead, pink reluctantly agreed."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Split with Dr. Luke
podcast.body: Pink publicly stated that she no longer works with Dr. Luke, calling him "not a good person," and offered her support to singer Kesha during Kesha's abuse lawsuit against him. "She no longer works with Dr. Luke, however, has called him, quote, not a good person, and supported singer Kesha in her later abuse lawsuit against Dr. Luke."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Teen Pop Era Origins
podcast.body: Pink emerged from the teen pop era, but quickly pivoted to an R&B star before transitioning to a more rock-oriented sound. "emerged from the teen pop era as an R&B star, then pivoted to a more rock-oriented sound."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
